1.title: From Business Problem to Claude Solution
1.text: Welcome to Module one: From Business Problem to Claude Solution. This module covers from business problem to claude solution. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. How to turn a vague business ask into a testable problem statement. How to decide whether Claude is the right tool and which solution shape fits. The five business value pillars and how to attach measurable targets to them. How to frame constraints and risks before design starts.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory and the Bank That Wants "AI for Customer Service"
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory and the Bank That Wants "A I for Customer Service". A retail bank's executive says: "We want A I in customer service.". Lumen's architect asks what hurts: average handle time, inconsistent answers, after-hours coverage, cost per contact. The ask becomes: draft replies for agents from the policy library, with citations, cut handle time twenty-five percent, no regulated advice without review.

1.title: From Ask to Problem Statement
1.text: From Ask to Problem Statement. A business ask is a wish; a problem statement names who, what, how well, under which constraints.

1.title: From Ask to Problem Statement, continued
1.text: From Ask to Problem Statement, continued. The figure shows this: From a vague ask to a testable problem statement: who is affected, what hurts, how it is measured today, which constraints apply, and a target with an owner.

1.title: From Ask to Problem Statement, continued
1.text: From Ask to Problem Statement, continued. Users and workflow. Question: Who will use it, in which process step? Bank example: Contact-center agents drafting replies. Pain and baseline. Question: What is wrong today, in numbers? Bank example: nine-minute handle time, fourteen percent rework. Success criteria. Question: What result counts as success, measurably? Bank example: twenty-five percent faster, ninety-five percent policy-correct. Constraints. Question: Latency, cost, data, regulation, platform, skills. Bank example: Customer P I I, region rules, budget per contact. Risks. Question: What happens when it is wrong? Bank example: Wrong fee advice reaches a customer. Ownership. Question: Who accepts, runs and funds it? Bank example: Head of service operations.

1.title: From Ask to Problem Statement, continued
1.text: From Ask to Problem Statement, continued. Success criteria first. Specific, measurable, achievable and relevant criteria are the basis of later evals (Module eleven). Translate language to metrics: "faster" becomes handle time; "accurate" becomes policy-correct rate on a test set. Fit check: L L M s (large language model) suit language-heavy, variable, judgment-assisted work; they are a poor first choice for exact, rule-bound calculation, hard real-time control, or tasks where a simple rule or classic model is cheaper and fully reliable. Exam tip: The first architect move on a vague request is discovery that produces measurable success criteria and constraints, not choosing a model or a framework.

1.title: Choosing the Solution Shape
1.text: Choosing the Solution Shape. The figure shows this: Climb only as far as the problem needs: a single optimized call, then a workflow, then an augmented L L M with retrieval and tools, then an agent or multi-agent system.

1.title: Choosing the Solution Shape, continued
1.text: Choosing the Solution Shape, continued. Single optimized call. Use when: Task fits one prompt with good context and examples. Cost and risk: Lowest. Workflow (chain, route, parallel). Use when: Steps are known; each can be checked. Cost and risk: Low; predictable. Augmented L L M (retrieval, tools, memory). Use when: Needs your data or actions. Cost and risk: Medium; integration and security work. Agent or multi-agent. Use when: Path cannot be predicted in advance. Cost and risk: Highest; compounding errors, four times to fifteen times tokens. Simplest solution that works: add complexity only when it demonstrably improves the measured outcome. Build, buy or configure: use built-in product features where they meet the need; build custom only for differentiating or constrained cases.

1.title: Choosing the Solution Shape, continued
1.text: Choosing the Solution Shape, continued. Plan where a human reviews: draft-and-review is usually the first production pattern for risky outputs.

1.title: Business Value Pillars
1.text: Business Value Pillars. The guide names five pillars. Tie every design choice to at least one and give it a number.

1.title: Business Value Pillars, continued
1.text: Business Value Pillars, continued. Efficiency. Meaning: Same output with less time or effort. Example target: Handle time down twenty-five percent. Typical design lever: Draft generation, retrieval of policy. Transformation. Meaning: New capability or redesigned process. Example target: Instant multilingual support. Typical design lever: New workflow, agentic process. Productivity. Meaning: More output per person. Example target: Analyst reviews three times more files. Typical design lever: Summarization, extraction. Cost. Meaning: Lower total cost to serve. Example target: Cost per contact down thirty percent. Typical design lever: Smaller model, caching, batch. Performance S L A s (service level agreement). Meaning: Meet speed, availability, quality commitments. Example target: p ninety-five latency under three seconds, ninety-nine point nine percent uptime. Typical design lever: Streaming, routing, capacity planning.

1.title: Business Value Pillars, continued
1.text: Business Value Pillars, continued. The figure shows this: Five value pillars with a measure and a design lever each: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance S L A s. Pillars conflict: a larger model may raise quality but lift cost and latency. State the priority order with the client. Quantify benefit and cost early (tokens per request times volume, review effort, integration work) to test the business case. Exam tip: A design justified by a named pillar with a measurable target is stronger than one justified by "better A I". When pillars conflict, the answer states the trade-off and the client's priority.

1.title: Constraints That Shape the Design
1.text: Constraints That Shape the Design. Data sensitivity and regulation. Platform and region choice, Z D R or B A A, P I I masking (Module fourteen). Latency. Streaming, smaller model, caching, routing (Module ten). Volume and cost. Batch, caching, model tiering (Modules four, six, twelve). Existing systems. Integration path: A P I (application programming interface), M C P (Model Context Protocol), queue (Modules seven, eight). Team skills and operations. Managed services, simpler patterns, runbooks (Module sixteen). Accuracy and risk tolerance. Evals, human review, guardrails (Modules eleven, thirteen). Exam tip: Pillars conflict (quality against cost and latency): the strong answer names the trade-off and the client's priority.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. First move: Discovery to measurable success criteria and constraints. Problem statement: Users, pain and baseline, target, constraints, risks, owner. Fit: Language-heavy, variable work; not exact calculation or hard real-time. Shapes: Single call, workflow, augmented L L M, agent or multi-agent. Rule: Simplest that works; climb only on evidence. Pillars: Efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance S L A s. Conflict: State the trade-off and the client's priority. Human review: Plan it where errors are costly.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A client says "we want A I in customer service." What should the architect do first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Measurable criteria and constraints must exist before architecture choices.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A task has fixed steps, each easy to check, and low tolerance for unpredictability. Which shape fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Known steps favor a predictable workflow over an agent.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An executive wants an "A I transformation" but cannot name a metric. Which response is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Business value must be measurable to guide design and to judge success.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which task is the weakest fit for an L L M as the core component? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Exact, rule-bound calculation belongs in deterministic code; the L L M can orchestrate or explain.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A larger model raises quality but breaks the p ninety-five latency target. How should the architect proceed? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Pillars conflict; make the trade-off explicit and test options against it.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two belong in a problem statement before design begins? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Targets and constraints frame the design; implementation details come later.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. When is a multi-agent design most justified? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Multi-agent systems cost many more tokens and suit parallelizable, high-value work.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. The bank wants to cut cost per contact. Which design lever most directly serves the cost pillar? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Caching and tiering reduce the cost per request without discarding needed context.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: A. Question four: B. Question five: A. Question six: B and E. Question seven: C. Question eight: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
